source.title: Mixtures of Experts Unlock Parameter Scaling for Deep RL
source.authors: Johan Obando-Ceron; Ghada Sokar; Timon Willi; Clare Lyle; Jesse Farebrother; J. Foerster; G. Dziugaite; D. Precup; Pablo Samuel Castro

page_placements.theme: Reinforcement-learning scaling depends on architecture, difficulty and allocation

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws but studies RL agent performance, not held-out language-model loss, power-law fits, extrapolation of loss, or compute-optimal allocation. Its RL performance results are a related but different measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports RL performance as parameter count is varied, but does not measure cross-entropy loss or fit or test power laws. Those RL performance results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than linked to a claim version. It cites language-model scaling laws as context; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study scales value-based RL agents by adding MoE experts (1–8) and reports Atari game scores (IQM human-normalized). It does not measure held-out pretraining loss and fits no power law. It does not test extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation or shape at fixed parameters, and does not link downstream performance to scale or loss. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. The RL score-versus-parameters results measure a related but different construct (task score under architecture-dependent widening), so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that naively scaling RL network parameters hurts performance. Adding MoE modules, especially Soft MoE, to value-based agents makes them more parameter-scalable across training regimes, which they present as evidence toward developing RL scaling laws. They do not fit or establish any scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales RL agent architectures and measures game scores; it does not use the language-model loss measurement or fitting procedures in the cited scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling outcome differs by MoE type: Soft MoE gains increase with expert count, while Top1-MoE does not show that scaling behavior. The paper also explores replay ratio, tokenization, encoder, expert dimensionality, game suite, and training regime.

fits_no_version.finding: In DQN and Rainbow on 20 ALE games, naively widening the penultimate layer reduces score (Rainbow about −40% from 1× to 8×). Soft MoE scores rise with expert count (Rainbow +20% from 1 to 8 experts). Top1-MoE helps only Rainbow and does not improve with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In value-based deep RL, whether added parameters improve task performance depends on architecture. Naive widening hurts, while Soft MoE lets performance grow with expert count.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix F: with SAC and PPO on MuJoCo, Soft MoE gives no significant gain or loss, and Top1-MoE degrades performance. With Atari 100k training (100k interactions), MoE variants show no real difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE-enabled parameter scaling gains in RL depend on the domain, network type and training length.

record.code_released: The paper says the code is public, but no study-code URL is stated in the text.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: The results concern RL game scores rather than the language-model held-out loss in the claim. Many plotted values are not given numerically in the text; confidence intervals are shown but exact bounds are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other RL performance experiments and analyses (Figures 4–20 and Sections 4.2–5.3) are not included because they concern MoE design choices, training regimes, or representation/runtime measures rather than the claim’s language-model loss, extrapolation, compute allocation, or power-law form.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss; no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute split between parameters and data.
No comparison of loss across depth or width at fixed parameter count. Figure 5's expert-dimension result is an RL score with MoE structure varied, not LM loss.
Only RL game scores at 1/2/4/8 experts. No loss metric and no power-law form fitted or tested in RL.
No relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss or LM scale.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: For r1 and r2 (the Soft MoE scaling trend), the natural baseline is the 1-expert Soft MoE configuration. The record's baseline field describes the width-matched dense comparator instead; this is minor. None of the rows measures loss, and no power-law form is fitted, so no version receives a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger-run loss are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is evaluated.
No language-model loss comparison varying depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study examines RL performance under parameter scaling, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in RL or another modality or training regime.
No downstream-task performance relationship to pretraining loss or language-model scale is evaluated.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, fitting choices, or bending loss curves are examined.

rows.subject: DQN
rows.size_stated: Parameter count increased by increasing the number of experts; each expert copies the original penultimate layer.
rows.stage_stated: deep reinforcement learning; trained for 200M environment steps
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the penultimate layer with Soft MoE and varied the number of experts.
rows.baseline: Baseline architecture; the corresponding layer is scaled by the number of experts to approximately match parameters.
rows.value: Soft MoE provides clear performance gains, and the gains increase with the number of experts (Figure 1).
rows.uncertainty: 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals are shown; exact bounds not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the trend, but does not give numeric DQN scores.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim versions; DQN Soft MoE gains increase with expert count, but no power-law form is tested.
source_check.problem: The reported RL-score trend is correct, but observed is inappropriate for a row linked to no claim version.

relation.reason: Scaling laws motivate the work, which is presented as evidence toward developing RL scaling laws rather than establishing or testing one.

tranche.reason: The study measures RL game-score changes with architecture size; it neither tests the specified power-law forms nor uses a fitted scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. The row-state corrections concern their meaning relative to the catalog versions; the reported RL-score trends and percentages are supported.
